synopsis: South Africa's Regulation 8.10 was promulgated in 2015 and is described as the strongest explicit off-road automatic-braking mandate found in the research, but an expert account says it was also suspended in 2015 because the technology was unavailable; the supplied facts do not resolve its subsequent status [f2272, f2277, f10855]. Its wording covers diesel-powered trackless mobile machines at mines where a risk assessment identifies the stipulated significant collision risk, while coverage of battery-electric machines remains unclear [f2279, f2280]. The regulation publishes no detection percentage, metres-to-object threshold, false-alarm limit or fixed stopping-distance test, consistent with a case-study account that it specified what must be done but not how [f2281, f10856]. Mines check validation and site-acceptance evidence against Regulation 8.10 and MOSH requirements, which include independent verification at two readiness gates [f1614, f12289, f15094]. The research recommends treating South African mine compliance as a design input even when South Africa is not the launch market [f2278].

relations.note: Both describe mines checking evidence against Regulation 8.10 and MOSH requirements.
Locates the evidence-checking requirement specifically in site acceptance.
Adds independent verification at two readiness gates to the acceptance framework.
Missing quantitative tests substantiate the account of specifying what, not how.
The strongest identified mandate motivates incorporating South African compliance into design.
Defines the machine and risk-assessment scope of the identified mandate.
Flags unresolved battery-electric coverage alongside explicit diesel wording.
Adds reported suspension and technology-unavailability context to the promulgation year.
Reported suspension creates unresolved tension with characterization as the strongest mandate.
Qualifies compliance-led design: the regulation supplies no fixed quantitative acceptance thresholds.
